points.guide: Molecular theory in solids, liquids and gases.
aims: Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Name the changes of phase and explain them with the particle model.

slides.title: Particles in three phases
bullets: Solid: a fixed lattice. Particles only vibrate, so the shape and volume are fixed
Liquid: particles close but disordered. They vibrate and move past one another, so only the volume is fixed
Gas: particles far apart and fast, with almost no forces except in collisions
Gases compress easily because of the space between particles; solids and liquids barely compress
slides.notes: An elementary explanation is all the guide asks for. Water is the unusual case: ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

slides.title: Changing phase
bullets: Solid to liquid: melting (reverse: freezing). Some intermolecular bonds break, so particles can move about
Liquid to gas: boiling or evaporation (reverse: condensing). Most of the remaining bonds break
Solid straight to gas: sublimation (reverse: deposition, as when frost forms)
Every one of these changes can be reversed
slides.notes: The guide lists melting, freezing, boiling, condensing and evaporation. Sublimation and deposition are extra vocabulary from the lesson deck.

aims: Calculate density, mass or volume with $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$, using SI units.

slides.title: Density
bullets: Density is mass per unit volume, in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$
Particles touch in solids and liquids, so their densities are high; gases are roughly 1000 times less dense
Conversions: $1\ \text{g cm}^{-3} = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ and $1\ \text{cm}^{3} = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}$
slides.notes: Density comes back in convection (fluids of different density) and in the gas laws of B.3.

slides.title: Is the ring pure gold?
slides.question: A ring has a mass of 11.2 g. Lowered into a narrow measuring cylinder of water, it raises the reading by 0.70 $\text{cm}^{3}$. Pure gold has a density of 19 300 $\text{kg m}^{-3}$. (a) Find the density of the ring in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$. (b) State whether the ring can be pure gold.
slides.hint: The rise in the reading is the volume of the ring. Change the mass to kilograms and the volume to cubic metres before dividing.

steps.text: The volume is the rise in the reading.
(a) Divide the mass by the volume.
(b) This is well below 19 300 $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, so the ring is not pure gold.

slides.notes: A density near 16 000 kg m⁻³ is typical of 18-carat gold, which is alloyed with lighter metals.

points.guide: The internal energy of a system is the total intermolecular potential energy arising from the forces between the molecules plus the total random kinetic energy of the molecules arising from their random motion.
aims: Define internal energy in terms of the random kinetic and intermolecular potential energies of the molecules.
Distinguish between temperature and internal energy.

slides.title: Internal energy
bullets: Molecules have random kinetic energy because they vibrate, slide or fly about
They have intermolecular potential energy because of the forces between them
Internal energy = total random kinetic energy + total intermolecular potential energy
Supplying thermal energy makes the molecules move faster, or moves them further apart, or both
An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so all of its internal energy is kinetic
slides.notes: Only random motion counts: a ball thrown across the room has extra kinetic energy as a whole, but its molecules are no hotter. Springs between atoms make a helpful picture of the potential energy part.

slides.title: Temperature or internal energy?
bullets: Temperature tells us about the average kinetic energy per particle
Internal energy is a total, so it depends on how much substance there is
A swimming pool at 25 °C has far more internal energy than a mug of tea at 80 °C
A thermometer responds to the kinetic part only: a potential energy change does not show on it
slides.notes: Ask which holds more internal energy: 1 kg of ice at 0 °C or 1 kg of water at 0 °C. The temperature is the same, but the water has more potential energy.

points.guide: Kelvin temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles of an ideal monatomic gas as given by $\overline{E}_k = \tfrac{3}{2}k_B T$.
aims: Relate the kelvin temperature to the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Calculate average kinetic energies with $\overline{E}_k = \tfrac{3}{2}k_B T$.

slides.title: Average kinetic energy of a particle
bullets: $\overline{E}_k$ is the average kinetic energy of one particle, in J
$k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}$ is the Boltzmann constant
$T$ must be the absolute temperature, in kelvin
Particles in a gas have a wide range of speeds: this is the average over all of them
slides.notes: The equation is given without proof here. B.3 connects it to the pressure of a gas.

slides.title: Which gases does it describe?
bullets: It is stated for an ideal monatomic gas, such as helium, neon or argon
A single atom can only move from place to place, so all its kinetic energy is translational
Molecules with several atoms rotate and vibrate as well, so they hold more kinetic energy in total
For any ideal gas, $\tfrac{3}{2}k_B T$ is still the average translational kinetic energy per molecule

slides.title: A helium weather balloon
slides.question: The helium in a weather balloon is at 220 K high in the atmosphere. Treat helium as an ideal monatomic gas. Find (a) the average kinetic energy of a helium atom and (b) how many times greater the average kinetic energy was on the ground, when the helium was at 293 K.
slides.hint: The average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature, so part (b) needs only a ratio of temperatures.
slides.notes: This average depends only on the temperature, not on the size of the balloon. A larger balloon has more atoms and so more internal energy, at the same temperature.

points.guide: Kelvin and Celsius scales are used to express temperature.
aims: Explain how extrapolating gas measurements leads to absolute zero and the kelvin scale.
Convert between kelvin and Celsius temperatures.

slides.title: From Celsius to kelvin
bullets: The Celsius scale $\theta$ is fixed by the freezing and boiling points of water
The kelvin scale $T$ starts at absolute zero: 0 K is $-273$ °C
Write 300 K, not 300 °K: the kelvin has no degree sign
Physics equations involving absolute temperature need kelvin
slides.notes: More precisely, absolute zero is −273.15 °C, but the data booklet uses 273.

slides.title: Where the 273 comes from
slides.start: Heat a fixed sample of gas in a sealed, rigid container. Its pressure $p$ is a straight-line function of its Celsius temperature $\theta$.

steps.text: Each sample of gas gives a straight line
Extend the line back to zero pressure
Every sample of every gas gives the same value
So $p_{0} = 273a$, and the line can be written
Define $T = \theta + 273$: pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature

slides.notes: Here $a$ is the gradient and $p_{0}$ is the pressure at 0 °C. Pressure cannot be less than zero, so this temperature is the lowest possible. The straight line through the origin returns in B.3 as the pressure law.

slides.title: Finding absolute zero
bullets: Each line is one sample of gas, heated at constant volume
Measurements cover only a small range; the rest of each line is extrapolated
All the lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature

points.guide: The change in temperature of a system is the same when expressed with the Kelvin or Celsius scales.
aims: Explain why a temperature change has the same value in kelvin and in degrees Celsius.

slides.title: A temperature change
bullets: The degrees on the two scales are the same size; the scales are simply shifted by 273
So warming by 30 °C is the same as warming by 30 K
A change $\Delta T$ may be written in either unit, but $T$ on its own needs kelvin in physics equations

slides.title: Liquid nitrogen
slides.question: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K, and the air in a laboratory is at 20 °C. Find (a) the boiling point of nitrogen in °C, (b) the temperature of the air in K and (c) the difference between the two temperatures, on each scale.
slides.hint: The two scales differ by a fixed 273, and one kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius.
slides.notes: The 273 cancels when two temperatures are subtracted. This is why Q = mcΔT works in either unit, while the equations with T on its own need kelvin.

points.guide: Quantitative analysis of thermal energy transfers $Q$ with the use of specific heat capacity $c$ as given by $Q = mc\Delta T$.
aims: Solve problems with $Q = mc\Delta T$, including electrical heating and mixing.
Determine a specific heat capacity from heating data.

slides.title: Specific heat capacity
bullets: $c$ is the energy needed per kilogram for each kelvin of temperature rise, in $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
Each material has its own value: equal masses given equal energy warm by different amounts
$\Delta T$ can be in K or °C, because it is a change
Water has an unusually large value, about 4200 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$, which is why seas warm and cool so slowly
slides.notes: Values of c are given in exam questions when they are needed.

slides.title: The gradient of a heating graph
slides.start: A heater of constant power $P$ warms a mass $m$ of a substance. No energy is lost to the surroundings.

steps.text: The energy supplied by the heater in a time $t$
The energy gained by the substance
Divide by $mct$: the gradient of the temperature–time graph

slides.notes: A steeper gradient means a smaller specific heat capacity. An electric heater also gives P = VI, so the energy can be calculated from Q = VIt.

slides.title: Using the equation
bullets: Find $\Delta T$ first, and take care to use the mass in kilograms
From an electric heater: $Q = Pt$ or $Q = VIt$
When objects mix with no losses, the energy given out by the hotter equals that taken in by the cooler
The objects end at one shared final temperature
In an electrical heating experiment, losses to the surroundings make the calculated $c$ too large
slides.notes: Students should write the mixing equation with (higher temperature − lower temperature) on each side, so that both sides are positive.

slides.title: An electric shower
slides.question: An electric shower has a 9.0 kW heater. Cold water enters at 12 °C and leaves at 40 °C. All the electrical energy warms the water. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. Find (a) the mass of water flowing through each second and (b) the mass of water delivered in one minute.
slides.hint: Power is the energy transferred each second, so write the equation for one second of flow.

steps.text: In one second the heater supplies 9000 J.
(a) Solve for the mass heated each second.

slides.notes: About 4.6 litres a minute, which is why electric showers feel weaker than mains-pressure ones. Turning the temperature up reduces the flow.

slides.title: A pan in the sink
slides.question: An aluminium pan of mass 0.80 kg at 90 °C is placed in a sink holding 5.0 kg of water at 35 °C. Energy transfer to the surroundings is negligible. The specific heat capacities are 900 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ for aluminium and 4200 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ for water. Find the final temperature of the water.
slides.hint: Call the final temperature $T$. The energy lost by the pan equals the energy gained by the water.

steps.text: Energy lost by the pan = energy gained by the water.

slides.notes: The water barely warms up: it has about six times the mass and more than four times the specific heat capacity of the pan.

slides.title: Measuring c for cooking oil
slides.question: A 300 W heater warms 0.50 kg of cooking oil. The temperature of the oil rises steadily from 20 °C to 56 °C in 120 s. (a) Find the specific heat capacity of the oil. (b) State and explain whether the true value is likely to be larger or smaller than your answer.
slides.hint: Find the gradient of the temperature–time graph first. For part (b), think about where some of the energy goes.

steps.text: The gradient of the temperature–time graph.
(b) Some energy escapes, so the oil warms by less than the calculation assumes. The answer is too large: the true value is smaller.

slides.notes: The same reasoning applies to any electrical measurement of c. Insulating the container reduces the error.

points.guide: A phase change represents a change in particle behaviour arising from a change in energy at constant temperature.
aims: Explain, in terms of molecular energies, why the temperature stays constant during a phase change.
Sketch and interpret graphs of temperature against energy supplied or time.

slides.title: What happens during a phase change
bullets: Energy is still being supplied, but the temperature stays constant
The average kinetic energy is unchanged, so the energy goes into potential energy
The energy does work against the attractive forces between the molecules
A helpful picture: a molecule trapped in a deep box gains height until it can climb out and is free
When a substance freezes or condenses, potential energy falls and the same energy is released
slides.notes: Temperature only reveals the kinetic part of the internal energy, so a flat section means no change in the average kinetic energy.

slides.title: Heating ice until it is steam
bullets: Slopes: one phase warming, kinetic energy rising
Flat sections: a phase change, potential energy rising
Boiling takes longer than melting, as separating the molecules completely needs more energy
slides.notes: At constant power, the time axis is proportional to the energy supplied.

points.guide: Quantitative analysis of thermal energy transfers $Q$ with the use of specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization of substances $L$ as given by $Q = mL$.
aims: Solve problems with $Q = mL$, including those with several stages.
Compare boiling and evaporation.

slides.title: Specific latent heat
bullets: $L$ is the energy that takes 1 kg from one phase to another at constant temperature, in $\text{J kg}^{-1}$
$L_f$ (fusion) is for melting and freezing; $L_v$ (vaporization) is for boiling and condensing
The energy absorbed in one direction is released in the other
Use $Q = mL$ on the flat sections of a heating curve and $Q = mc\Delta T$ on the slopes
slides.notes: "Latent" means hidden: no temperature change reveals the energy being transferred.

slides.title: Boiling and evaporation
bullets: Boiling: at one fixed temperature for a given pressure, with bubbles appearing all through the liquid
Evaporation: at any temperature, and only from the surface
Only the most energetic molecules escape, so the average kinetic energy of the rest falls: evaporation cools the liquid
It is faster with a warmer liquid, a larger surface area or moving air
slides.notes: Sweating works this way. Ask why a wet swimsuit feels cold on a windy day.

slides.title: Freezing an ice tray
slides.question: An ice tray holds 0.40 kg of water at 15 °C. A freezer removes energy from it at an average rate of 40 W. Find the time taken for the water to become ice at $-18$ °C. Use 4200 and 2100 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ for the specific heat capacities of water and ice, and $3.34 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ for the specific latent heat of fusion.
slides.hint: Split the cooling into stages. How many stages are there, and which involve a change in temperature?
slides.notes: Freezing takes about three-quarters of the energy, although it happens at a single temperature.

slides.title: A barista's steam wand
slides.question: Steam at 100 °C is blown into 0.25 kg of milk at 5 °C. All the steam condenses, and the milk and condensed water end at 65 °C. Use 3900 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ for milk, 4200 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ for water and $2.26 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ for the specific latent heat of vaporization of water. Energy losses are negligible. Find the mass of steam needed.
slides.hint: The steam gives out energy in two stages. Write each as an expression in the unknown mass, then set the total equal to the energy gained by the milk.

steps.text: Energy from cooling the condensed water to 65 °C.
Solve for the mass of steam.

slides.notes: Only 24 g of steam is needed, because condensing releases so much energy. The same fact makes steam scalds so severe.

slides.title: Cooling a cyclist
slides.question: During a hard ride, a cyclist's skin loses 0.80 kg of sweat by evaporation in one hour. At skin temperature the specific latent heat of vaporization of sweat is $2.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$. Find the average rate at which evaporation removes energy from the cyclist.
slides.hint: Find the energy for the whole hour first, then divide by the number of seconds in an hour.

steps.text: The energy needed to evaporate the sweat.

slides.notes: Over 500 W is comparable with the waste power of a cyclist working hard. Sweat that drips off removes almost no energy: it has to evaporate.

points.guide: Conduction, convection and thermal radiation are the primary mechanisms for thermal energy transfer.
aims: Name the three main mechanisms of thermal energy transfer and state what each one needs.

slides.title: Three ways to transfer thermal energy
bullets: Conduction: through matter, while the matter itself stays in place
Convection: by the movement of a fluid (a liquid or a gas)
Thermal radiation: by electromagnetic waves, which need no medium
Only radiation can carry the energy of the Sun to us through empty space
slides.notes: A wood-burning stove shows all three: the iron conducts, air currents move around the room, and you feel radiation from across the room. Ask which of the three could still cross the vacuum in a vacuum flask.

points.guide: Conduction in terms of the difference in the kinetic energy of particles.
aims: Explain conduction in terms of the kinetic energy of particles.
Explain why metals conduct well and gases conduct poorly.

slides.title: How conduction works
bullets: Particles in the hot region have more kinetic energy than those in the cold region
In collisions they pass on kinetic energy to neighbours with less, all along the material
Energy travels, but the particles stay where they are
Metals conduct very well: their free electrons carry energy quickly through the lattice
Gases conduct poorly, because their particles are so far apart: trapped air insulates
slides.notes: Free electrons also explain why good electrical conductors tend to be good thermal conductors. A metal bench feels colder than a wooden one on the same morning because it conducts energy away from the hand faster.

points.guide: Temperature difference determines the direction of the resultant thermal energy transfer between bodies.
aims: Use temperature differences to predict the direction of the net thermal energy transfer.
Define thermal equilibrium.

slides.title: Which way does the energy go?
bullets: The net transfer is always from the higher temperature to the lower
Internal energy does not decide it: a small hot nail warms a large bath of cool water
The hot body cools and the cold body warms until the temperatures match
Thermal equilibrium: equal temperatures, and no net transfer of energy
Objects contain internal energy; "heat" is energy in transit. Cold never flows in
slides.notes: At equilibrium, energy still passes both ways between the bodies, but at equal rates, so the net transfer is zero.

points.guide: Quantitative analysis of rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction in terms of the type of material and cross-sectional area of the material and the temperature gradient as given by $\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = -kA\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$.
aims: Calculate the rate of energy transfer by conduction with $\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = -kA\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$.

slides.title: Rate of conduction
bullets: $k$ is the thermal conductivity of the material, in $\text{W m}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$
$A$ is the cross-sectional area; $\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$ is the temperature gradient
The minus sign shows that energy flows towards the colder side
In calculations, use the size of $\Delta T$ and put $\Delta x$ in metres
slides.notes: The conduction equation has the same form as the flow of electric charge, which is useful in B.5.

slides.title: Conduction through a slab
bullets: A larger area gives a larger rate of energy transfer
A larger temperature difference gives a larger rate
A thicker slab gives a smaller rate
A material with larger $k$ gives a larger rate

slides.title: Insulating a loft
slides.question: A ceiling of area 60 $\text{m}^{2}$ is covered with mineral wool 0.27 m thick, with thermal conductivity 0.040 $\text{W m}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. The temperature is 20 °C at the bottom of the wool and 2 °C at the top. Find (a) the rate of energy transfer through the wool and (b) the thickness of wool that would reduce this rate to 100 W.
slides.hint: Use only the size of the temperature difference. For part (b), rearrange the equation for the thickness.

steps.text: (a) Use the size of the rate.

slides.notes: The rate is inversely proportional to the thickness, so reducing 160 W to 100 W needs 1.6 times the thickness.

points.guide: Qualitative description of thermal energy transferred by convection due to fluid density differences.
aims: Describe how differences in fluid density set up a convection current.

slides.title: Convection currents
bullets: Convection needs a fluid: it cannot happen in a solid
A heated fluid expands, so its density falls
Warm fluid, being less dense, rises; cooler fluid of greater density sinks and takes its place
The rising fluid cools, sinks and is heated again: a convection current
"Heat rises" is wrong: it is the warm fluid that rises
slides.notes: Only a qualitative description is required: there are no convection calculations in this topic.

slides.title: A convection current
bullets: Convection also shapes the planet and the stars:
thunderclouds and weather systems
ocean currents
hot rock in the mantle, moving tectonic plates
the churning surface of the Sun
slides.notes: Rock in the mantle flows extremely slowly: over millions of years it behaves as a very viscous fluid. Plate tectonics itself is not in the guide.

points.guide: The emission spectrum of a black body and the determination of the temperature of the body using Wien's displacement law as given by $\lambda_{\max} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$ where $\lambda_{\max}$ is the peak wavelength emitted.
aims: Describe how the emission spectrum of a black body changes with temperature.
Use Wien's displacement law to find a body's temperature or peak wavelength.

slides.title: Thermal radiation and black bodies
bullets: Every object above 0 K emits thermal radiation: electromagnetic waves from its surface
At everyday temperatures, the radiation is mostly infrared
A black body absorbs every bit of radiation reaching it and reflects nothing
No surface at the same temperature can emit more than a black body
Stars behave almost like black bodies; dark, matt surfaces are closer than light, shiny ones
slides.notes: A solid looks the colour of the light it does not absorb. A black body absorbs every wavelength, yet it glows when hot enough. Emissivity, which describes real surfaces, is in B.2.

slides.title: Wien's displacement law
bullets: $\lambda_{\max}$ is the wavelength at the peak of the spectrum, in m
$T$ is the temperature of the surface, in K
Measuring the peak wavelength of a star gives its surface temperature
Cool stars look red; very hot stars look blue-white

slides.title: Black-body spectra
bullets: Hotter: more power at every wavelength
The area under a curve is the total power emitted per unit area of surface
Hotter: the peak moves to shorter wavelengths
Heated metal goes from a dull red through orange to yellow-white

slides.title: A lamp filament and a star
slides.question: The filament of an old-style lamp is at 2700 K. A star's spectrum peaks at a wavelength of 290 nm. Find (a) the peak wavelength emitted by the filament, stating the region of the spectrum it lies in, and (b) the surface temperature of the star.
slides.hint: Wien's law links the two quantities with one constant. Rearrange it for each part, and put the wavelength in metres.

steps.text: Evaluate: this is longer than visible light, so it is in the infrared.

slides.notes: Most of the power from a filament lamp is emitted in the infrared, which is why these lamps waste so much energy. A star at 10 000 K looks blue-white.

points.guide: Quantitative analysis of energy transferred by radiation as a result of the emission of electromagnetic waves from the surface of a body, which in the case of a black body can be modelled by the Stefan-Boltzmann law as given by $L = \sigma AT^{4}$ where $L$ is the luminosity, $A$ is the surface area and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the body.
aims: Calculate the luminosity of a black body with $L = \sigma AT^{4}$.
Express and compare luminosities in watts and in terms of the luminosity of the Sun.

slides.title: The Stefan–Boltzmann law
bullets: Luminosity $L$ means radiated power, in W: the total power emitted by a body
$\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\,\text{K}^{-4}$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant
$A$ is the surface area and $T$ is in kelvin; for a sphere, $A = 4\pi R^{2}$
Doubling $T$ multiplies $L$ by $2^{4} = 16$
Star luminosities may be given in W or as multiples of the Sun's luminosity, $L_{\odot}$
slides.notes: No body is at 0 K, so every body radiates. The law gives the power emitted; the net power loss also depends on what the body absorbs from its surroundings (B.2).

slides.title: Comparing a star with the Sun
slides.start: Treat a star and the Sun as black spheres, of radius $R$ and $R_{\odot}$, with surface temperatures $T$ and $T_{\odot}$.

steps.text: The surface area of a sphere
In the same way, for the Sun

slides.notes: A star can be very luminous either because it is very hot or because it is very large.

slides.title: A white dwarf
slides.question: A white dwarf has a radius of $5.8 \times 10^{6}$ m and a surface temperature of 25 000 K. Treat it as a black body. Taking $L_{\odot} = 3.8 \times 10^{26}$ W, find its luminosity (a) in watts and (b) in terms of the luminosity of the Sun.
slides.hint: A star is a sphere, so find its whole surface area first. Check that the temperature is raised to the fourth power.

steps.text: The surface area of the sphere.
(b) Divide by the luminosity of the Sun.

slides.notes: Very hot, but faint: a white dwarf is about the size of the Earth. Ask students what would be needed to make it as luminous as the Sun.

slides.title: A steel billet cools
slides.question: A steel billet with a surface area of 0.90 $\text{m}^{2}$ leaves a furnace at 1227 °C. Treat it as a black body. Find (a) the power it radiates and (b) the factor by which this power falls when the billet cools to 627 °C.
slides.hint: Convert both temperatures to kelvin before anything else. For part (b), everything except the temperature cancels in the ratio.
slides.notes: Using Celsius in the ratio would give about 15, instead of 7.7. Real hot steel has an emissivity of about 0.8 (B.2), so the true power is a little lower.

points.guide: Intensity as power per unit area, $I = \dfrac{P}{A}$; the concept of apparent brightness $b$, which is the intensity of a star's light where it is received.
aims: Define intensity and apparent brightness, and calculate intensity with $I = \dfrac{P}{A}$.

slides.title: Intensity
bullets: Intensity is the power falling on each unit of area, measured at right angles to the radiation, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$
Apparent brightness $b$ is the intensity of the light from a star where it is received
Luminosity is a property of the star; apparent brightness also depends on where you are observing from
slides.notes: New for exams from 2028. Intensity as I = P/A is in the 2028 data booklet.

slides.title: A laser pointer
slides.question: A laser pointer emits a beam of power 1.0 mW. The beam has a cross-sectional area of $2.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{2}$. Find the intensity of the beam.
slides.hint: Change the power to watts first, and then use the definition of intensity.
slides.notes: New for exams from 2028. A tiny power gives an intensity comparable with direct sunlight at the Earth's surface. The eye then focuses the beam to a tiny spot, so lasers must never be pointed at eyes.

points.guide: Luminosity $L$ of a body as given by $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}$.
aims: Derive and use $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}$.
Use luminosity and apparent brightness to find the distance to a star.

slides.title: Apparent brightness and luminosity
bullets: $b$ in $\text{W m}^{-2}$; $L$ in W; $d$ is the distance from the star, in m
An inverse-square law: at twice the distance, the brightness is a quarter as great
Two stars of equal luminosity: the closer one looks brighter

slides.title: Where the equation comes from
slides.start: A star of luminosity $L$ radiates equally in all directions, and nothing absorbs the energy on the way.

steps.text: At a distance $d$, the radiation has spread over a sphere of area
All of the power $L$ passes through that sphere
Brightness is intensity, power per unit area

slides.notes: The last step is the way astronomers use this: once L is known, a measured b gives the distance.

slides.title: The inverse-square law
bullets: The same light covers four times the area at twice the distance
Each square metre then receives a quarter of the power

slides.title: How far away is the star?
slides.question: A star has a luminosity of $40\,L_{\odot}$. Its apparent brightness measured at the Earth is $2.1 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. Taking $L_{\odot} = 3.8 \times 10^{26}$ W, find the distance of the star from the Earth.
slides.hint: Find the luminosity in watts, and rearrange the brightness equation for the distance.
slides.notes: This is about 25 light-years. Remind students to take the square root at the end.

slides.title: Solar power at Jupiter
slides.question: At the Earth's distance from the Sun, the solar panels of a space probe can produce 14 kW. Jupiter is 5.2 times further from the Sun than the Earth is. Assuming the panels work equally well in both places, find the power they can produce at Jupiter.
slides.hint: The power from the panels is proportional to the apparent brightness of the Sun. How does that depend on distance?

steps.text: The brightness falls with the square of the distance.
The power is proportional to the brightness.

slides.notes: No distances or luminosity are needed: the ratio does the work. Real probes to Jupiter need very large panels for this reason.
